name: table-count
description: Number of Drizzle pgTable() definitions across shared/. The mature-machine north star is a SMALLER schema (<=450 tables); today's count is far above it. This strict down-only ratchet makes the schema monotonic: adding a table fails CI until the baseline is deliberately bumped (a conscious 'yes we need this'), and every consolidation lowers the baseline toward the target. Founder-chosen 'strict' 2026-07-16.
lastBumpNote: 748 -> 749 on 2026-08-08: property_expenses (multifamily -> core Wave 3, migration 0221). NOI needs two axes and the product held only one: rent (the income axis, in the rent ledger) had a store, operating EXPENSE had none. So NOI was never computed, it was ASSUMED — the standing shortcut baked a flat ~40%-of-rent expense guess into every projection ('NOI ~= 60% of rent'), under which a building with a new roof and one with a failing roof produce the SAME NOI and the operator cannot see the very difference the product exists to manage; a cap rate or DSCR built on a guessed expense ratio is a fabricated number in a plausible costume. property_expenses is the LEDGER that replaces the guess with what the operator actually spent. Schedule-E-shaped: `category` is one of the fourteen IRS Schedule E (Form 1040) rental line items (shared/rental/propertyExpense.ts) — the vocabulary the operator already keeps their books in — of which two (mortgage_interest, depreciation) are stored for tax completeness but are NON-operating and excluded from NOI via the `is_operating` flag, which is derived SERVER-SIDE from isOperatingCategory(category), never client-set (so a financing cost can't be posted into the operating number) and stored rather than recomputed on read (so a later reclassification can't rewrite history's operating status). A completed maintenance ticket's invoice (maintenance_tickets.invoice_cents) rolls into this ledger via POST .../expenses/import-maintenance, and the roll-in must be re-runnable without double-charging: `source`/`source_ref` record which ticket a rolled row came from, and the PARTIAL UNIQUE (organization_id, source, source_ref) WHERE source_ref IS NOT NULL makes a re-run lose the INSERT (onConflictDoNothing) instead of posting the repair twice — partial on purpose, because manual rows carry a null source_ref and must stay unconstrained (two like-amount supply runs in a month are a real entry, not a duplicate). NO backfill and that is deliberate: there is no prior expense data to migrate, and seeding the 40% guess as fake rows would be the exact fabrication this table ends — it ships empty and fills only from real operator entry and the operator-invoked roll-in. Money posture (founder ruling 'be the rail, not the provider'): a LEDGER of money the operator ALREADY spent, on their own account, elsewhere — nothing here moves, holds, collects or charges a cent; amount_cents is a recorded fact, not a balance. Deliberate bump per this ratchet's own procedure. PRIOR NOTE -- 755 -> 748 on 2026-08-01: seven dead tables dropped by explicit founder ruling (picker) executing two standing deletion-ledger KILL rows plus the sessions cleanup. Dropped: sessions (Clerk JWT auth; no session-store package exists; zero readers/writers ever — the orgScopedDb test fixture that used it as its org-less example now pins jobLocks instead), satellite_snapshots + satellite_analysis (Satellite / Vision AI kill: routers, visionAI, computerVision, client page all deleted this commit), voice_calls + voice_call_recordings (Voice / AI voice kill: every writer deleted this commit; the two live read sites had their voice branches removed rather than left querying the unwritable), model_versions + training_metrics (ML registry: modelServing/modelTraining/dataQuality were unreached — their only 'importer' was the dead services/ai barrel, itself imported by nothing). DELIBERATELY NOT dropped, though the founder's nine-table authorization named them, because verification against code refuted the zero-reader/zero-writer premise: call_transcripts (live second voice pipeline: voiceCallAI.ts via routes-misc + routes-ai-operations) and compliance_alerts + regulatory_changes (live writer+reader complianceAI.ts via mounted /api/compliance). A drop that would break mounted code is a new founder decision, not an execution of an old one. Reduction locked in the same commit per this ratchet's own rule. PRIOR NOTE — 754 -> 755 on 2026-07-31: rental_units (migration 0219). The buy-and-hold vertical modelled a unit as `rental_leases.unit_label` — free text on a LEASE — and had no units table anywhere in the repo, so a unit only existed once somebody had leased it. Three verified defects follow directly. (1) Vacancy was invisible: GET /api/rent-roll/occupancy divides distinct (property_id, COALESCE(unit_label,'')) pairs holding an ACTIVE lease by the same pairs that have EVER held a lease, so a unit nobody has rented contributes 0 to the numerator AND 0 to the denominator and a half-empty building reports 100% occupied — the one number a landlord opens the rent roll to check was structurally incapable of showing the condition it exists to show. (2) The rent-roll importer did `if (u.isVacant) continue;`, discarding exactly the rows a landlord most needs, not out of carelessness but because there was nowhere to put a unit with no lease. (3) A statutory late-fee cap rode on a guess: `knownUnitCountFloor` says in its own comment that `properties` has no unit_count column so the only ground truth is DISTINCT units ever put on a lease — a FLOOR, never a count — and since Tex. Prop. Code §92.019 sets a different cap at 4+ units, proposeLateFee computed both branches and charged the lower, deliberately under-charging rather than risk an unlawful fee against a tenant. No rollup column can fix any of this: a vacant unit is a row that exists with NO lease, which is by definition unrepresentable on the lease table. ONE table, deliberately — there is NO `rental_buildings`, because `properties` already IS the building (one row per parcel, with square_feet and a structure_type enumerating sfr/duplex/triplex/fourplex/condo/townhouse/commercial/mixed_use/vacant_land) and a second building table would restate it and immediately drift, against this ratchet's own north star. `kind` (unit | pad | suite) is the discriminator that keeps a mobile-home park's ground-lease PAD and a strip centre's SUITE out of two more tables; `status` (active | offline | retired) keeps 'units I own' separable from 'units I could have leased', which is where occupancy numbers start lying. Backfilled — safely, and unlike 0218 which deliberately shipped none: this one only COPIES A LABEL ALREADY ON THE ROW (unit_label → rental_units.label, SFR leases getting 'Whole property' so occupancy math stops forking on null), inventing no fact. `rental_leases.unit_label` is retained as a denormalised display copy because it is read in 20+ places including raw SQL in two route files. Deliberate bump per this ratchet's own procedure. PRIOR NOTE — 753 -> 754 on 2026-07-30: rent_payment_allocations (Wave D rent ledger, migration 0217). POST /api/leases/:id/payments credited the SINGLE oldest open charge (.limit(1)) and clamped the excess with max(0, amount + lateFee - paid), so a tenant two months behind who paid BOTH months had one month marked paid and the other still showing a full balance — while the ledger's own totals said the money arrived. Aging buckets, the late-fee decision, legal_posture, collected-% and the notice-to-vacate math all keyed off that wrong number, and a mis-stated balance in landlord/tenant court is not a display bug, it is the exhibit. A payment now spreads across every open charge (oldest first, rent before late fees) and each (payment, charge) line is PERSISTED, because in a dispute the question is never 'what is the balance', it is 'how did you get that balance': a tenant who paid $2,800 against three open months is entitled to know which month each dollar cured and how much went to a late fee rather than to rent. That is per-(payment, charge) data with a per-line rent/fee split — no aggregate on rent_charges or rent_payments can reconstruct it after the fact, so a rollup column cannot do this job. Rows are append-only (written inside the payment transaction, never mutated) and the UNIQUE (payment_id, rent_charge_id) index IS the double-apply guard, the same way ach_debit_attempts_period_uidx is the double-charge guard on the borrower side. Deliberate bump per this ratchet's own procedure. PRIOR NOTE — 756 -> 753 on 2026-07-29: platform money-custody purge (founder ruling "be the rail, not the provider", migration 0214). transaction_fee_settlements, fee_payout_schedules and fee_audit_log were the storage for server/services/transactionFeeService.ts — a platform escrow-and-take-a-cut engine (collect a buyer/seller/platform fee, HOLD it on AcreOS's balance for N days, release, transfer out) that had ZERO call sites. Nothing ever wrote a row and nothing ever read one, and processPayout() stamped a fabricated `tr_simulated_<ts>` id into a money column. Customer money never moves on AcreOS's own account, so the tables have no future either: dropped rather than frozen. A REDUCTION, which this ratchet's own rule requires be locked in the same commit. PRIOR NOTE — 754 -> 756 on 2026-07-29: ach_mandates + ach_debit_attempts (founder ruling #12(c) Wave C — ACH mandate/autopay, migration 0213). The borrower portal shipped an autopay Switch that wrote ONE boolean (notes.auto_pay_enabled) and scheduled nothing; the flag's only reader was cashFlowForecaster, which FORECAST money that was never collected while the portal told the borrower "Autopay is on — we will collect this payment automatically". Two things a boolean cannot carry each need a table. (1) ach_mandates: NACHA §2.3 requires the Originator to obtain AND RETAIN the Receiver's authorization for every consumer debit and produce it on demand — the verbatim text shown, its version, agreed_at, IP/UA, the dollar ceiling and frequency authorized, and the processor's corroborating mandate id. A rollup column cannot answer "what exactly did this borrower authorize, and when". (2) ach_debit_attempts: one row per (note, period, attempt), where the unique index IS the double-charge guard — a duplicate job run, a double-click, or a crash-and-retry all lose the insert BEFORE money moves, and the same key is replayed as the processor idempotency key. Return codes (R01-R29), the bounded re-presentment ladder, and the reversal linkage all hang off the attempt, so a returned debit is auditable instead of a mutated status. Deliberate bump per this ratchet's own procedure. PRIOR NOTE — 753 -> 754 on 2026-07-29: note_payoff_quotes (Wave C 'Money moves', migration 0212). A payoff statement is a representation the note holder is legally bound by, and AcreOS computed payoff quotes in three places — with three different day-count behaviours — while persisting NONE of them. When a closer wires the quoted figure and the ledger disagrees to the cent, nothing recorded what was quoted, as of what date, or from which inputs, so there was no way to establish which side moved. No rollup column can answer that; the quote EVENT (full engine input snapshot alongside its output, immutable, one row per quote issued) needs a table. It deliberately spans BOTH note books via note_system + note_ref, so unifying the borrower-portal quote onto the same engine needs no second table. Deliberate bump per this ratchet's own procedure. PRIOR NOTE — 752 -> 753 on 2026-07-29: mail_qr_scan_events (Wave B 'Wire the engine', migration 0211). The direct-mail attribution funnel was a capable-looking UI over permanent zeros — qr_scan_count was read in 8 places and written in 0, with no QR generation and no scan endpoint. The rollup column alone cannot answer 'why is this number what it is', and a QR redirect that silently swallows bot/prefetch hits without recording them is just a different kind of unaccountable number, so the scan EVENTS (counted and deliberately-not-counted alike, each with a reason) get a table. Everything else in that migration is additive columns/indexes on existing tables. Deliberate bump per this ratchet's own procedure.
